fields: Do Not Start With This When

rows.Main Input: single-cell or high-resolution spatial omics samples with expression and coordinates
rows.Main Use in This Topic: cross-sample spatial matching and alignment at single-cell resolution
rows.Main Output: matched cells or spots and aligned spatial correspondence map
rows.Key Difference: Uses search-and-match correspondence at high resolution rather than primarily fitting a global transport plan, diffeomorphic warp, or latent embedding.
rows.Evidence Note: Direct PubMed evidence verifies the Nature Methods method paper, PMID 39294367 and DOI 10.1038/s41592-024-02410-7. Scale sensitivity is a Layer 2 synthesized caution. Targeted 2026-05-02 code-link check verified a public repository: https://github.com/wanglab-broad/CAST.
rows.Best First Choice When: When high-resolution spatial omics samples need cell-level search-and-match correspondence across samples.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When the task is simple spot-level consensus alignment, count batch correction, or multimodal tissue modeling rather than high-resolution matching.

rows.Main Input: spatiotemporal transcriptomics samples with expression, coordinates, and time or progression structure
rows.Main Use in This Topic: alignment across spatial and temporal transcriptomics states
rows.Main Output: spatiotemporally aligned correspondence or trajectory map
rows.Key Difference: Adds explicit spatiotemporal alignment logic to transport-based integration rather than treating all slices as unordered static sections.
rows.Evidence Note: Direct PubMed evidence verifies the Cell Systems method paper, PMID 39874960 and DOI 10.1016/j.cels.2024.12.001. Resource and scale labels are Layer 2 synthesis from the transport family and registry compute label. Targeted 2026-05-02 code-link check verified a public repository: https://github.com/raphael-group/DeST_OT.
rows.Best First Choice When: When the Integration question has an ordered temporal or developmental component, not only static slice registration.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When there is no temporal or progression structure to preserve and a simpler pairwise slice alignment is enough.

rows.Main Input: spatial genomics datasets with expression features and coordinates
rows.Main Use in This Topic: non-rigid alignment through smooth spatial warping
rows.Main Output: aligned spatial coordinates or latent spatial mapping
rows.Key Difference: Models non-rigid spatial variation with Gaussian-process structure rather than optimal transport, graph attention, or diffeomorphic metric mapping.
rows.Evidence Note: Direct PubMed evidence verifies the Nature Methods method paper, PMID 37592182 and DOI 10.1038/s41592-023-01972-2. The high scale-sensitivity label is Layer 2 synthesis from the Gaussian-process alignment family, not a BioHarness benchmark. Targeted 2026-05-02 code-link check verified a public repository: https://github.com/andrewcharlesjones/spatial-alignment.
rows.Best First Choice When: When smooth non-rigid spatial warping is the central selection cue.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When the main goal is batch correction, multimodal factor modeling, or very large high-resolution matching without a scale audit.
rows.Cross-Sample Cue: same-platform or related spatial genomics samples

rows.Main Input: spatial expression matrix and spatial graph or coordinates
rows.Main Use in This Topic: spatially informed representation integration linked to clustering and deconvolution workflows
rows.Main Output: integrated representation or embedding with downstream clustering/deconvolution support
rows.Key Difference: Uses self-supervised graph contrastive representation learning and is cross-topic because integration is one of several explicit outputs.
rows.Evidence Note: Direct PubMed evidence verifies PMID 36859400 and DOI 10.1038/s41467-023-36796-3, and the frozen registry supplies the primary GitHub link. Its Integration role and scale/resource cautions are Layer 2 synthesis because the method also serves clustering and deconvolution.
rows.Best First Choice When: When integrated spatial representation is needed together with downstream clustering or deconvolution interpretation.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When the primary requirement is an explicit coordinate transform, slice stitching, or 3D reconstruction.

rows.Main Input: multiple spatial transcriptomics slices with expression and spatial coordinates
rows.Main Use in This Topic: pairwise slice alignment and consensus integration
rows.Main Output: aligned slices and consensus slice representation
rows.Key Difference: Canonical optimal-transport route for multi-slice alignment when slices are broadly comparable rather than partially overlapping.
rows.Evidence Note: Direct PubMed evidence verifies PMID 35577957 and DOI 10.1038/s41592-022-01459-6, and the frozen registry supplies the primary GitHub link. Benchmark papers use PASTE as an important baseline, but branch placement is Layer 2 synthesis.
rows.Best First Choice When: When comparable spatial transcriptomics slices need pairwise alignment or a consensus slice baseline.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When only partial tissue overlap is expected, when temporal ordering is central, or when the goal is count batch correction.

rows.Main Input: multiple spatial transcriptomics slices with partial overlap or missing regions
rows.Main Use in This Topic: partial alignment for multislice spatially resolved transcriptomics
rows.Main Output: partial slice alignment and matched overlapping regions
rows.Key Difference: Extends the PASTE family to partial overlap, making it a better branch candidate when tissue sections do not share full correspondence.
rows.Evidence Note: Direct PubMed evidence verifies the Genome Research paper, PMID 37553263 and DOI 10.1101/gr.277670.123, and the frozen registry supplies the primary GitHub link. Partial-overlap preference is direct from method scope, while burden labels are Layer 2 synthesis.
rows.Best First Choice When: When multi-slice spatial transcriptomics sections only partially overlap or include missing tissue regions.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When full-slice consensus alignment, latent representation integration, or non-spatial batch correction is the actual task.

rows.Main Input: multiple spatial transcriptomics samples with expression and coordinates
rows.Main Use in This Topic: joint probabilistic embedding, clustering, and alignment for spatial data integration
rows.Main Output: integrated embedding, aligned samples, and cluster labels
rows.Key Difference: Couples probabilistic embedding with clustering and alignment rather than focusing only on coordinate registration.
rows.Evidence Note: Direct PubMed evidence verifies PMID 36653349 and DOI 10.1038/s41467-023-35947-w. Comparator/resource labels are Layer 2 synthesis. Targeted 2026-05-02 code-link check verified a public repository: https://github.com/feiyoung/PRECAST.
rows.Best First Choice When: When integration should jointly support embedding and clustering across multiple spatial transcriptomics samples.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When the scientific question needs an explicit geometric transform, stitching, or 3D reconstruction before clustering.

rows.Main Input: spatial omics sections or fields requiring alignment and stitching
rows.Main Use in This Topic: coarse-to-fine alignment and stitched tissue reconstruction
rows.Main Output: stitched and aligned spatial omics map
rows.Key Difference: Targets alignment plus stitching, making it more natural for section or field assembly than latent-only integration methods.
rows.Evidence Note: Direct PubMed evidence verifies the Nature Communications method paper, PMID 39025895 and DOI 10.1038/s41467-024-50308-x. Benchmark inclusion supports relevance, while scale burden remains Layer 2 synthesized. Targeted 2026-05-02 code-link check verified a public repository: https://github.com/leihouyeung/SANTO.
rows.Best First Choice When: When the Integration task is explicitly about coarse-to-fine alignment and stitching of spatial omics sections.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When the goal is latent representation harmonization, count batch correction, or multimodal factor modeling.

rows.Main Input: heterogeneous spatial transcriptomics slices with expression and spatial structure
rows.Main Use in This Topic: alignment of heterogeneous slices through spatial-linked correspondence
rows.Main Output: aligned heterogeneous slices and correspondence links
rows.Key Difference: Emphasizes heterogeneous-slice alignment rather than full-overlap optimal transport or general latent batch correction.
rows.Evidence Note: Direct PubMed evidence verifies PMID 37945600 and DOI 10.1038/s41467-023-43105-5. Benchmark inclusion supports relevance; heterogeneity and relative-placement cautions remain Layer 2 synthesis. Targeted 2026-05-02 code-link check verified a public repository: https://github.com/gao-lab/SLAT.
rows.Best First Choice When: When slices are heterogeneous and need spatial-linked alignment rather than ordinary comparable-slice registration.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When the task is simple full-overlap alignment, count batch correction, or multimodal tissue-complexity modeling.

rows.Main Input: spatial transcriptomics slices with expression, coordinates, and optional image or architecture context
rows.Main Use in This Topic: 3D slice alignment and tissue architecture stacking through the SPACEL framework
rows.Main Output: aligned 3D tissue architecture or stacked spatial map
rows.Key Difference: Provides a broader deep-learning tissue-architecture framework rather than only a pairwise alignment or batch-correction method.
rows.Evidence Note: Direct PubMed evidence verifies PMID 37990022 and DOI 10.1038/s41467-023-43220-3, and the frozen registry supplies the primary GitHub link. Its 3D Integration role is Layer 2 scoped to the Scube-style alignment/stacking part of a broader framework.
rows.Best First Choice When: When the Integration problem is tissue architecture reconstruction or 3D stacking rather than only pairwise slice alignment.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When a lightweight CPU baseline, explicit pairwise transport alignment, or count-level batch correction is required first.

rows.Main Input: spatial transcriptomics data with coordinates and optionally cross-technology spatial maps
rows.Main Use in This Topic: coordinate-framework alignment through diffeomorphic metric mapping
rows.Main Output: diffeomorphic transform and aligned spatial coordinates
rows.Key Difference: Prioritizes smooth invertible geometric mapping rather than transport matching or latent representation correction.
rows.Evidence Note: Direct PubMed evidence verifies PMID 38065970 and DOI 10.1038/s41467-023-43915-7, and the frozen registry supplies the primary GitHub link. Cross-technology and geometry-risk cues are Layer 2 synthesis from method scope.
rows.Best First Choice When: When the main requirement is a coordinate transform that preserves a smooth tissue geometry model.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When the task is latent batch correction, multimodal molecular integration, or single-cell search-and-match alignment.

rows.Main Input: multiple spatial transcriptomics datasets across conditions, technologies, or stages
rows.Main Use in This Topic: graph-attention integration across samples, conditions, technologies, and developmental stages
rows.Main Output: integrated embedding and aligned spatial domains
rows.Key Difference: Targets cross-condition, cross-technology, and developmental-stage integration more directly than generic graph representation methods.
rows.Evidence Note: Direct PubMed evidence verifies PMID 38177758 and DOI 10.1038/s43588-023-00528-w, and the frozen registry supplies the primary GitHub link. Benchmark support strengthens in-scope status, but ordering versus other graph methods is only branch-local Layer 2 synthesis.
rows.Best First Choice When: When the key Integration cue is harmonizing spatial transcriptomics across conditions, technologies, or developmental stages.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When explicit geometric warping, stitching, or partial-overlap pair matching is the primary deliverable.

rows.Main Input: serial spatial transcriptomics sections for alignment, integration, and 3D reconstruction
rows.Main Use in This Topic: end-to-end spatial transcriptomic alignment, integration, and 3D reconstruction
rows.Main Output: aligned integrated sections and reconstructed 3D tissue map
rows.Key Difference: Combines alignment, integration, and 3D reconstruction in one method identity rather than separating registration from reconstruction.
rows.Evidence Note: Direct PubMed evidence verifies PMID 41398698 and DOI 10.1186/s13059-025-03895-x. Scale and audit caution are Layer 2 synthesis from the end-to-end 3D scope. Targeted 2026-05-02 code-link check verified a public repository: https://github.com/yuyuanyuana/STAIR.
rows.Best First Choice When: When the stated task needs alignment, integration, and 3D reconstruction considered together.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When a simpler audited pairwise alignment baseline is sufficient or model-opacity and scale-burden caveats are unacceptable for first-pass audit.

rows.Main Input: serial spatial transcriptomics sections with expression, coordinates, and inter-section continuity cues
rows.Main Use in This Topic: dense 3D atlas reconstruction with virtual-slice generation from planar spatial transcriptomics sections
rows.Main Output: dense 3D cell atlas and in silico virtual sections
rows.Key Difference: Builds a dense 3D atlas that supports in silico virtual slicing rather than stopping at aligned or stacked sections alone.
rows.Evidence Note: Direct publisher evidence verifies the Nature Methods article DOI 10.1038/s41592-025-02969-9 with online publication on 2025-12-31, and code availability points to the public Spatial-Z repository. Layer 2 synthesis: branch placement emphasizes 3D atlas reconstruction and virtual slicing rather than generic slice alignment or super-resolution.
rows.Best First Choice When: When the deliverable is dense 3D atlas reconstruction or in silico virtual-slice generation from serial planar spatial transcriptomics sections.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When the task is only pairwise slice alignment, count batch correction, or low-resolution same-section super-resolution rather than 3D atlas building.

rows.Main Input: multi-slice and multi-condition spatial transcriptomics datasets
rows.Main Use in This Topic: interpretable joint representation for multi-slice and multi-condition integration
rows.Main Output: joint integrated representation with interpretability hooks
rows.Key Difference: Uses masked self-supervised graph-style representation for multi-slice, multi-condition integration rather than explicit coordinate registration.
rows.Evidence Note: Direct PubMed evidence verifies PMID 41194133 and DOI 10.1186/s13059-025-03850-w. Relative placement versus other graph methods remains Layer 2 synthesized. Targeted 2026-05-02 code-link check verified a public repository: https://github.com/maiziezhoulab/MaskGraphene.
rows.Best First Choice When: When the central need is multi-slice, multi-condition joint representation with an interpretability emphasis.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When the output must be a geometric transform, stitched map, or count-level batch-corrected matrix.

rows.Main Input: single-slice and multi-slice spatial transcriptomics datasets
rows.Main Use in This Topic: contrastive unified analysis across single-slice and multi-slice data
rows.Main Output: unified spatial representation for single-slice and multi-slice analysis
rows.Key Difference: Frames integration as unified contrastive analysis across both single-slice and multi-slice settings.
rows.Evidence Note: Direct PubMed evidence verifies PMID 40551235 and DOI 10.1186/s13059-025-03636-0. Scale burden is not resolved by the bounded PubMed check. Targeted 2026-05-02 code-link check verified a public repository: https://github.com/EnchantedJoy/spCLUE.
rows.Best First Choice When: When the workflow needs a single contrastive integration frame that covers both single-slice and multi-slice spatial transcriptomics analysis.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When the first deliverable must be explicit slice coordinates, 3D structure, or a conservative CPU batch-correction baseline.

rows.Main Input: multi-slice spatial transcriptomics data for 2D or 3D integration
rows.Main Use in This Topic: automated integration of multi-slice data in 2D and 3D
rows.Main Output: integrated 2D or 3D multi-slice spatial map
rows.Key Difference: Emphasizes automated 2D/3D integration rather than a single low-level alignment primitive.
rows.Evidence Note: Direct PubMed evidence verifies PMID 40598307 and DOI 10.1186/s13059-025-03630-6. Automation benefit and audit risk are Layer 2 synthesis. Targeted 2026-05-02 code-link check verified a public repository: https://github.com/Ramialison-Lab/VR-Omics.
rows.Best First Choice When: When the method-selection cue is automated 2D/3D integration of multi-slice spatial transcriptomics data.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When transparent low-level alignment primitives or count-level batch correction are preferred for first-pass review.

rows.Main Input: multimodal spatial omics data from tissue sections
rows.Main Use in This Topic: multimodal spatial omics integration for resolving tissue complexity
rows.Main Output: multimodal tissue-complexity model or integrated representation
rows.Key Difference: Targets multimodal spatial omics modeling rather than transcriptomics-only slice alignment or batch correction.
rows.Evidence Note: Direct PubMed evidence verifies PMID 39815104 and DOI 10.1038/s41592-024-02574-2. Its inclusion is branch-specific to multimodal Integration; resource burden remains a conservative Layer 2 cue. Targeted 2026-05-02 code-link check verified a public repository: https://github.com/kpcoleman/miso.
rows.Best First Choice When: When multiple spatial omics modalities need to be integrated to model tissue complexity.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When the input is transcriptomics-only and the immediate need is slice registration, stitching, or count batch correction.

rows.Method Family: Batch correction for single-cell spatial transcriptomics
rows.Main Input: single-cell spatial transcriptomics count data across batches or samples
rows.Main Use in This Topic: count-level batch correction and cross-sample harmonization
rows.Main Output: batch-corrected count data or corrected representation for visualization and spatial gene pattern analysis
rows.Key Difference: Focuses on batch correcting single-cell spatial count data rather than aligning tissue geometry or reconstructing 3D structure.
rows.Evidence Note: Direct PubMed evidence verifies PMID 40001084 and DOI 10.1186/s13059-025-03479-9. The decision to isolate it as the batch-correction branch is Layer 2 synthesis from its method scope. Targeted 2026-05-02 code-link check verified a public repository: https://github.com/immunogenomics/crescendo.
rows.Best First Choice When: When the Integration task is specifically batch correction of single-cell spatial transcriptomics count data.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When spatial coordinate alignment, stitching, 3D reconstruction, or multimodal tissue modeling is the main deliverable.

rows.Main Input: spatial multi-omics datasets with partially observed modalities across samples or tissue sections
rows.Main Use in This Topic: integrate mosaic spatial multi-omics data while preserving spatial and cross-modality structure
rows.Main Output: integrated spatial multi-omics representation and modality-completion or harmonized feature outputs
rows.Key Difference: Targets mosaic spatial multi-omics settings where not every modality is measured in every sample, rather than ordinary slice alignment or transcriptomics-only batch correction.
rows.Evidence Source: PubMed PMID 42032296; DOI 10.1038/s41588-026-02573-3; code link supplied by targeted literature check
rows.Evidence Note: Direct evidence verifies the Nature Genetics SpaMosaic method-paper identity and public code trace. Branch placement as mosaic multi-omics Integration is direct from the title; resource and scale labels are conservative Layer 2 synthesis.
rows.Best First Choice When: When the Integration task is mosaic spatial multi-omics integration with missing or partially paired modalities across samples.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When the main deliverable is coordinate registration, single-modality batch correction, or cell type annotation rather than mosaic multi-omics integration.
rows.Primary Risk Cue: modality imbalance and cross-modality imputation bias

rows.Main Input: multiple spatial transcriptomics datasets from diverse sources with expression and spatial context
rows.Main Use in This Topic: integrate heterogeneous spatial transcriptomics datasets with interpretable spatially aware modeling
rows.Main Output: integrated representation and interpretable spatial factors or components for cross-dataset comparison
rows.Key Difference: Emphasizes flexible and interpretable spatially aware integration across diverse spatial transcriptomics sources rather than explicit coordinate warping or 3D reconstruction.
rows.Evidence Source: PubMed PMID 42045691; DOI 10.1038/s41588-026-02579-x; code link supplied by targeted literature check
rows.Evidence Note: Direct evidence verifies the Nature Genetics INSPIRE method-paper identity and public code trace. Interpretability and diverse-source integration are direct title cues; comparator and resource fields are Layer 2 synthesis.
rows.Best First Choice When: When heterogeneous spatial transcriptomics datasets need interpretable spatially aware integration rather than only geometric alignment.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When the required output is a diffeomorphic coordinate transform, stitched section, or molecular modality-completion model.

rows.Method Family: Spatial continuous mapping and cross-omics correction
rows.Main Input: spatial multi-omics data requiring continuous spatial mapping and cross-omics correction
rows.Main Use in This Topic: perform spatial continuous mapping and cross-omics correction for spatial multi-omics integration
rows.Main Output: cross-omics corrected representation and continuous spatial mapping outputs
rows.Key Difference: Focuses on continuous spatial mapping plus cross-omics correction, separating it from pure multimodal representation learning or transcriptomics-only batch correction.
rows.Evidence Source: PubMed PMID 41991905; DOI 10.1038/s41467-026-71882-2; code link supplied by targeted literature check
rows.Evidence Note: Direct evidence verifies the Nature Communications SpatialCOC method-paper identity and public code trace. Cross-omics correction is direct method scope; risk cues are Layer 2 synthesis.
rows.Best First Choice When: When the Integration problem is explicitly cross-omics correction with spatial continuous mapping.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When the task is only slice alignment, ordinary count-level batch correction, or cell type annotation.

rows.Main Input: single-cell and spatial omics data with expression features suitable for interpretable gene-program modeling
rows.Main Use in This Topic: integrate and annotate single-cell and spatial omics data using interpretable gene programs
rows.Main Output: integrated representation, gene-program factors, and annotation-supporting outputs
rows.Key Difference: Uses interpretable gene programs for robust single-cell/spatial integration and annotation, making it a boundary row with Cell Type Inference, Program Discovery, and Domain / Clustering.
rows.Evidence Source: DOI 10.1016/j.xgen.2025.101105; Cell Genomics method paper; code link supplied by targeted literature check
rows.Evidence Note: Direct DOI/publisher evidence verifies SSpMosaic as a Cell Genomics method for single-cell/spatial omics integration and annotation using interpretable gene programs. Layer 2 includes it in Integration while preserving boundaries to Cell Type Inference, Program Discovery, and Domain / Clustering/ecotype interpretation.
rows.Best First Choice When: When integration and annotation are coupled through interpretable gene programs and the analysis can explicitly track the program/annotation boundary.
rows.Do Not Start With This When: When the primary task is standalone cell type inference, program discovery, or domain/ecotype discovery rather than integration.
